blocks.text: Romans 16 reveals a network of women and men whose work included carrying messages, hosting assemblies, writing letters, laboring, traveling, suffering imprisonment, and supporting others. These descriptions are not interchangeable job titles: the chapter uses different language for service, support, coworking, labor, hosting, and apostleship. Tertius's first-person greeting also distinguishes Paul's responsibility for the letter from Tertius's physical work of writing it.

A household was more than a modern private residence; it belonged to a social fabric shaped by household authority, shared practices, patronage, and public or civic relationships. The assembly in Prisca and Aquila's house and the groups associated with Aristobulus and Narcissus therefore point to social networks as well as places where people gathered.

Cenchreae was Corinth's eastern port, while Lechaeum faced west; together Corinth's ports connected sea routes with north-south land travel. This makes Phoebe's location and the wider movement of coworkers geographically concrete, although Romans never supplies her itinerary. Roman gathering spaces could include houses, multi-storey dwellings, shops, workshops, warehouses, or rented rooms of very unequal size and control; no excavated site can be securely identified as one of the assemblies greeted here.

Paul commends Phoebe as sister, diakonos, and prostatis and asks the recipients to welcome and assist her. The terms can be translated in ways that carry different assumptions about service, office, patronage, benefaction, or protection. Commendation practice makes it probable that she carried or represented the letter and may have helped interpret it, but the text never explicitly says that she transported the document or defines a modern job description for her.

The greetings suggest several distinguishable groups rather than one clearly described centralized congregation: an assembly meets in Prisca and Aquila's house, while other people are grouped with named individuals or households. The list does not reveal an exact number of congregations, their venues, boundaries, demographics, or governance. Likewise, the names alone cannot securely classify individuals as enslaved, freed, elite, migrant, or connected with famous imperial households.

Junia is best understood as a woman's name. The phrase concerning Andronicus and Junia may mean that they were prominent among the apostles or that they were well known to the apostles; the grammar remains disputed. The uncertainty should be preserved without turning Junia into a man merely to exclude a woman from the apostolic question. More broadly, Mary, Tryphaena, Tryphosa, Persis, Prisca, Phoebe, and other women are named with differentiated forms of labor and agency, not as a single undifferentiated category.

A Latin pavement inscription near the Corinthian theater records an Erastus who paid for paving in connection with civic office. It illustrates how public office and benefaction could be linked, but it does not securely prove that its donor was the Erastus called the city's treasurer in verse 23. The possible identification also cannot establish the social class of everyone in the Corinthian or Roman assemblies.

The doxology printed in verses 25-27 appears in different locations, or is absent, in parts of the manuscript tradition. This variation witnesses to the letter's circulation history, but by itself it does not prove a particular shorter first edition. Interpretations that use the doxology to settle the structure of Romans should therefore acknowledge the textual question.

The papyri labeled P10, P26, P27, P31, P40, P46, and P61 preserve different portions of Romans; the labels do not imply that the manuscripts have equal date, extent, or textual weight. P46 is by far the most extensive early papyrus witness, yet it is not Paul's original document and its readings still require comparison with other witnesses. Major codices such as Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, and Claromontanus also have distinct omissions, corrections, and textual profiles.

The surrounding discussion distinguishes gifts, maintenance, wage analogies, hospitality, partnership, collection, obligation, civic benefaction, and labor. Treating all of them simply as patronage would erase who gives to whom, on what occasion, and for what stated purpose. That distinction helps keep the collection in chapter 15, Phoebe's assistance, Gaius's hosting, and Erastus's civic role from being forced into one economic model.

sections.title: Romans in Its Wider Textual and Economic Context
